newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Multinationals to sell stakes to Zimbabwe blacks.
newsitem.headline: Multinationals to sell stakes to Zimbabwe blacks.

text.p: Some multinational companies, including Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd, have agreed to sell "significant fractions" of their shares in Zimbabwean firms to local black investors, President Robert Mugabe said in an interview with the official Herald newspaper.

Mugabe said two cabinet ministers were negotiating the details of the deals with the multinationals -- including Lonrho Plc, which the government wants to offer equity to its black managers. The sales would support the government's programme to empower economically the majority black population.
Anglo and Lonrho officials were not immediately available for comment.

"Some multinationals have agreed to sell significant fractions of their shareholdings in Zimbabwean companies to indigenous (black) investors as part of the major government thrust to indigenise the economy," the Herald quoted Mugabe as saying.
"The government has been targeting selected multinationals with extensive holdings in Zimbabwe," he said.

Mugabe praised mining giant Anglo which earlier this year offered to sell 20 percent of its shares in Bindura Nickel Corporation to the government. The government hopes to warehouse the shares for black investors when it eventually buys them.
But he said the government also wanted Anglo to appoint more black Zimbabweans to run its companies because it was already pushing black advancement in its home base, South Africa.
Mugabe said the government was also talking to Lonrho to offer black managers equity in the group, but said he found Lonrho chief executive Dieter Bock difficult to understand.
"With his (Bock's) background in real estate, he had admitted that he had no experience of managing mines, factories and agricultural concerns," he said.

Mugabe said the government considered it a failure that it could not stop some non-indigenous (white) Zimbabweans and offshore shareholders from buying Union Carbide Corp's smelter in Kwekwe in central Zimbabwe.

"The government would have preferred this group to have brought in indigenous (black) Zimbabweans as well and kept the company in this country," he said of the smelter which has set up its headquarters in Mauritius.
"Dividends are now being paid to persons who claim to be Zimbabweans," Mugabe said.
